list.listitem: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a vascular retinopathy that develops only in premature infants with outcomes anywhere from normal vision to blindness. Incidence decreases with increasing birth weight and gestational age.

Infants with a birth weight of less than 1500 g or 30 weeks' gestational age or less and selected infants with birth weights of 1500 to 2000 g or greater than 30 weeks' gestational age with an unstable clinical course should have retinal screening examinations. The DIGIROP online risk score is well validated. B
Oral propranolol reduces the risk of requiring treatment for ROP (NNT=18). B
Peripheral retinal ablation via laser therapy or cryotherapy is used to ablate the entire peripheral avascular retina in infants with severe ROP. A
Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VGEF) antibodies are also effective but have higher recurrence rates. B
ROP regresses and heals in about 80% of cases. C

Supplementation with an enteral oil that included 100 mg/kg/day of arachidonic acid and 50 mg/kg/day of docosahexaenoic acid until 40 weeks post-menstrual age significantly reduced the likelihood of severe ROP (NNT = 6). B

background.definition: ROP is a vascular retinopathy that develops only in premature infants with outcomes anywhere from normal vision to blindness.

list.listitem: In infants born at less than 1251 g or less than 31 weeks' gestational age, the incidence is 58% to 68%.
The incidence decreases with increasing birth weight and gestational age.
A systematic review concluded that male infants were more likely to be treated for ROP.
Prematurity (84% incidence at <28 weeks' gestational age).

Liberal oxygen administration causes higher blood oxygen levels and variability of oxygen levels. A meta-analysis found that in infants less than 32 weeks' gestational age, early low oxygen saturation (70%-96%) and later high oxygen saturation (94%-99%) are associated with a lower risk of severe ROP. A large RCT compared target saturation of 85% to 89% with 91% to 95% and found no difference in either mortality or incidence of retinopathy of prematurity in a group of 1200 infants with gestational age 23 to 27 weeks.
Greater severity of illness.
Early administration of erythropoietin (at <8 days of life).
Not associated with increased risk: hyperglycemia, patent ductus arteriosus and its treatment (indomethacin or ligation), anemia or transfusion policies, and ambient lighting.

At 16 weeks' gestation, primitive capillaries grow into the inner retina, proceeding outward to the ora serrata, growing symmetrically from the optic disc, and reaching the nasal ora serrata at 35 to 40 weeks' gestation and the lateral ora serrata at 38 to 44 weeks' gestation.

An angiogenic growth factor, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), is normally produced by the avascular retina anterior to the advancing vessels, in response to tissue hypoxia, promoting neovascularization into that area.

Phase I ROP, hyperoxia-vasocessation phase, occurs in response to the administration of oxygen after birth for respiratory disease, which leads to decreased production of VEGF and cessation of vessel growth.
Phase II ROP, hypoxia-vasoproliferation phase, occurs in response to severe retinal hypoxia stimulating an increase in VEGF and in turn neovascularization.
See Diagnosis section and for screening and follow-up recommendations. B

A systematic review of 5 studies with 2208 preterm infants found low quality evidence that exclusive human milk feeding reduces the likelihood of ROP (OR 0.29; 95% CI 0.12-0.72). However, randomized trials are lacking, but are also unlikely.

A 2015 meta-analysis identified 5 trials that compared restricted O2 (SpO2 85%-89%) with liberal O2 (SpO2 91%-95%) policies. The likelihood of ROP was similar between groups, although there were other differences including mortality prior to hospital discharge (higher in the restricted O2 group).
There is no evidence that vitamin A supplementation prevents ROP.
The DIGIROP online risk score to identify newborns who should be screened for ROP is well validated.
An international classification system was designed to describe the retinopathy (see ). B

Retinal screening examinations in all infants with a birth weight of less than 1500 g or gestational age of 30 weeks or less and selected infants with birth weights of 1500 to 2000 g or more than 30 weeks' gestational age with an unstable clinical course. The DIGIROP online risk score is well validated.B

Conclude examinations when full retinal vascularization is reached, zone III retinal vascularization is attained without previous zone I or zone II ROP, postmenstrual age (gestational age plus chronologic age) of 45 weeks is reached and no prethreshold disease or worse ROP is present, or regression of ROP occurs. A
An international classification system was designed to describe the location and severity of retinopathy.

The Digital ROP prediction rool (DIGIROP-Screen) was developed in a cohort of 6991 patients 24 to 30 weeks gestational age, and validated in 1241 external groups. Sensitivity was nearly 100% (one infant in the validation group with severe malformations was incorrectly classified as not needing screening). Specificity was 53% at birth and 61% by 8 weeks. The DIGIROP-Screen tool requires only gestational age, birth weight, and gender and is available online.
The anterioposterior location of retinal involvement is described by 3 concentric zones centered around the optic disc (see ).

The extent of retinal involvement is described by clock hours where the 3-o'clock position is to the right and nasal in the right eye and temporal in the left eye, and the 9-o'clock position is to the left and temporal in the right eye and nasal in the left eye.

The severity of retinopathy is described by stages at the junction of the vascularized and avascular retina. If there are different stages represented within one eye, the most severe determines the staging for that eye (see ).
Plus disease indicates a more severe form of retinopathy and is defined by increased tortuosity and vascular engorgement of posterior retinal vessels in at least 2 quadrants of the eye.

Aggressive posterior ROP is a severe, rapidly progressive form of ROP seen in the extremely low-birth-weight infants that if untreated will lead to retinal detachment. This most commonly occurs in zone 1 and does not progress through the typical stages 1 to 3.

A smartphone based telemedicine screening for ROP for use in low to middle income countries had a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 84% (AUC 0.95) in a prospective study of 156 infants / 312 eyes.
See and Diagnostic Strategy section for a description of typical abnormal findings.

If a premature infant has been followed with retinal examinations, there are no other significant differential diagnoses. However, if an infant presents with retinal detachment, other causes of leukocoria, such as retinoblastoma and Norrie syndrome, will be in the differential.

Of note, there is an entity called familial exudative vitreoretinopathy, an autosomal dominant or X-linked recessive proliferative retinopathy that closely resembles ROP and should be in the differential if a term or near-term infant presents with what appears to be ROP.
Plus disease indicates a more severe form of retinopathy and is defined by increased tortuosity and vascular engorgement of posterior retinal vessels in at least 2 quadrants of the eye.

Aggressive posterior ROP is a severe, rapidly progressive form of ROP seen in the extremely low-birth-weight infants that if untreated will lead to retinal detachment. This most commonly occurs in zone 1 and does not progress through the typical stages 1 to 3.
A study of fellows found that 2 of 7 had a sensitivity less than 80% for detection of ROP.
An RCT found that 1 ml of oral 25% glucose solution 2 minutes before the ophthalmologic examination for ROP significantly reduced pain after the procedure (15.7% vs 68.5%, p < 0.001, NNT = 2).

Infants with a birth weight of less than 1500 g or gestational age of 30 weeks or less and selected infants with birth weights of 1500 to 2000 g or greater than 30 weeks' gestational age with an unstable clinical course should have retinal screening examinations.

Timing of the initial examination depends on the infant's postmenstrual age. Infants less than 28 weeks' gestational age should have the initial examination at 31 weeks' postmenstrual age. Infants of 28 weeks or more of gestational age should have the initial examination at 4 weeks of chronologic age.
Follow-up examinations are based on the retinal findings (see ).

Conclude examinations when full retinal vascularization is reached, zone III retinal vascularization is attained without previous zone I or zone II ROP, postmenstrual age of 45 weeks is reached and no prethreshold disease or worse ROP is present, or regression of ROP occurs.
Laser photocoagulation and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VGEF) antibodies are effective. The latter have higher recurrence rates. B
Oral propranolol reduces the risk of requiring treatment for ROP (NNT=18). B
For partial retinal detachments, vitrectomy and scleral buckling procedures have been performed with some improvement in visual and structural outcomes. C

Supplementation with an enteral oil that included 100 mg/kg/day of arachidonic acid and 50 mg/kg/day of docosahexaenoic acid until 40 weeks post-menstrual age significantly reduced the likelihood of severe ROP (NNT = 6). B

Laser photocoagulation is the traditional treatment for ROP, but intravitreal bevacizumab, an anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VGEF) monoclonal antibody, is also effective. However, the risk of ROP recurrence is higher and the American Academy of Ophthalmology report concludes that it should be used judiciously. This is based primarily on a systematic review of 5 RCTs.
Risk factors for ROP recurrence or reactivation include using ranibizumab, patent ductus arteriosus ligation, and requiring invasive mechanical ventilation on the day of therapy.
In trial randomizing 118 infants to intravitreal aflibercept or laser photocoagulation, treatment success at 24 weeks was 85.5% with aflibercept and 82.1% with photocoagulation.
Intraocular pressure increases following intravitreal injection of monoclonal antibodies, but a study of bevacizumab found it returned to normal within 15 minutes.
A dose de-escalation study concluded that 0.004 mg bevacizumab was the lowest effective dose.

A systematic review identified 3 studies with 366 patients with ROP comparing oral propranolol with placebo. Patients receiving beta-blockers had a lower risk of subsequently requiring an anti-VGEF agent (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.86, NNT = 18).
A small RCT (n = 63) of lutein found no benefit in preterm infants <32 weeks.
Laser photocoagulation is the standard therapy for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). Ablate the entire peripheral avascular retina using peripheral retinal ablation via laser therapy or cryotherapy.
A systematic review compared harms of laser therapy in infants treated for ROP. Astigmatism (OR 3.2, 95% CI 1.6 to 6.3) and myopia (OR 8.1, 95% CI 3.8 - 17) were more common following loaser therapy.

Criteria for treatment were revised in 2003 after the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) study that evaluated early treatment for high-risk prethreshold ROP versus conventional therapy for threshold ROP. The authors found improved visual and structural outcomes in those infants with type 1 ROP that were treated early. Type 1 ROP includes zone 1, any stage ROP with plus disease; zone 1, stage 3 ROP without plus disease; and zone 2, stage 2, or stage 3 ROP with plus disease.
For partial retinal detachments, vitrectomy and scleral buckling procedures have been performed with some improvement in visual and structural outcomes.
For total or near total retinal detachment, the visual outcomes are poor despite vitrectomy.

A study randomized 101 infants with a mean gestational age of 25.5 weeks (all < 28 weeks) to supplementation with an enteral oil that included 100 mg/kg/day of arachidonic acid and 50 mg/kg/day of docosahexaenoic acid or to no supplementation until 40 weeks post-menstrual age. Severe retinopathy was significantly less likely in the supplemented group (15.8% vs 33.3%, p = 0.02, NNT = 6). There was no difference in other outcomes including intraventricular hemorrhage or bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
An observational study found that fish-oil fat emulsions given intravenously are associated with a lower risk of ROP in very low-birth-weight infants, but clinical trials are lacking.
A systematic review of 4 studies with 800 very LBW infants found that while low dose vitamin A supplementation increased serum retinol concentrations, it had no effect on clinical outcomes.
ROP regresses and heals in about 80% of cases. C
Ablation therapy decreases unfavorable visual outcomes (best corrected visual acuity worse than 20/200) from 62% to 44% at 10-year follow-up (number needed to treat = 5). A
Do not transfer or discharge infants at risk for ROP until appropriate follow-up can be arranged. C
See Diagnosis section and for screening and follow-up recommendations.
Almost all infants born at less than 27 weeks' gestational age have ROP.
The likelihood of Type 1 ROP is 33% if ≤25 weeks gestation, 10% for 26 or 27 weeks, 4% for 28 or 29 weeks, and 0% if 30+ weeks.
ROP is usually visible as early as 4 weeks of postnatal age but is rarely seen before 31 weeks of postmenstrual age.
ROP regresses and heals in about 80% of cases.
The progression to retinal detachment is usually rapid once threshold disease is reached.
Ten percent of infants will progress to retinal detachment despite ablative treatment.
All infants with ROP, including those who never needed treatment, are at risk for visual impairment.

The Weight, IGF-1, Neonatal Retinopathy of Prematurity (WINROP) clinical algorithm can help identify infants at high risk for ROP.The ROPScore is another scoring system that predicts the likelihood of ROP, with area under the ROC curve of 0.77 for any ROP and 0.88 for severe ROP.
Ablation therapy decreases unfavorable visual outcomes (best corrected visual acuity worse than 20/200) from 62% to 44% at 10-year follow-up.
Do not transfer or discharge infants at risk for ROP until appropriate follow-up can be arranged.
Discharged infants should be followed serially by an ophthalmologist with experience and expertise in examining premature infants, until the ROP has resolved (see ).
Ophthalmology evaluation after discharge is indicated for all infants who had a history of ROP to follow for visual impairments.
